chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from al-Hasan ibn Sahl, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

He said: Indeed, Allah, the Exalted, is not a tyrant to His servant, but He tests him with whatever He wills. Among them is one He tests with illness, among them one He tests with poverty, among them one He tests with death, among them one He tests with hunger and thirst, among them one He tests with drought, among them one He tests with dominance, among them one He tests with wealth, among them one He tests with poverty, among them one He tests with illness, among them one He tests with health, among them one He tests with beauty, among them one He tests with ugliness, among them one He tests with knowledge, among them one He tests with ignorance, among them one He tests with strength, among them one He tests with weakness, among them one He tests with wealth, among them one He tests with poverty, to test which of you is best in deed.

key_terms.ظَلَّامٍ: Tyrant or one who deals unjustly

ai.seo_question: What is the wisdom behind Allah testing His servants with different types of trials?
ai.summary: In *Kamal al-Din*, Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elucidating the divine wisdom behind trials (*bala'*), emphasizing that afflictions like illness or poverty are not acts of injustice but precise tests to distinguish those who excel in good deeds. This concept aligns with the Shia understanding of *adl* (divine justice), where varied circumstances serve as a mechanism for spiritual refinement and the ultimate ranking of servants before Allah.
